subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A male neonate develops drooling, choking, and vomiting with his first feeding. The prenatal course was complicated by polyhydramnios. A chest radiograph shows a prominent gastric bubble, and a nasogastric tube cannot be passed into the stomach.
question: Which tracheoesophageal anomaly is the most common and produces a prominent gastric bubble?

options.text: Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula

explanation_correct: Esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula is the most common variant (about 85%). The atresia prevents swallowing of amniotic fluid, causing polyhydramnios, and neonates drool, choke, and vomit with the first feed. The distal fistula allows air to enter the stomach, producing a prominent gastric bubble on chest radiograph, and failure to pass a nasogastric tube into the stomach is a classic clinical test. It is associated with VACTERL defects, and cyanosis can occur from laryngospasm.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pure esophageal atresia produces a gasless abdomen because no air can reach the stomach, not a prominent gastric bubble.
explanation_incorrect.B: An H-type fistula has no atresia; it may have a relatively normal gas pattern and does not typically cause these severe feeding findings.
explanation_incorrect.C: Esophageal stenosis is not a tracheoesophageal fistula and would not explain distal air entry or the VACTERL association.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tracheal agenesis is not one of the tracheoesophageal anomalies described and would cause severe respiratory distress at birth.

educationalObjective: Esophageal atresia with distal TEF (85%) causes polyhydramnios, feeding-related choking, a prominent gastric bubble, and failure to pass an NG tube.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A neonate has excessive drooling and respiratory distress. An abdominal radiograph shows no gas in the stomach or bowel. A nasogastric tube coils in the upper esophagus.
question: Which tracheoesophageal anomaly produces a gasless abdomen on radiograph?
explanation_correct: In pure esophageal atresia (atresia or stenosis without a fistula), no air can pass from the trachea into the gastrointestinal tract, so the abdomen is gasless on radiograph. This contrasts with esophageal atresia with distal TEF, in which air entering through the fistula creates a prominent gastric bubble. The inability to pass a nasogastric tube into the stomach reflects the interrupted esophagus. Polyhydramnios and feeding intolerance are common.

explanation_incorrect.A: Esophageal atresia with distal TEF allows air into the stomach through the fistula, producing a prominent gastric bubble rather than a gasless abdomen.
explanation_incorrect.C: An H-type fistula is a side-to-side connection without atresia and does not cause a gasless abdomen.
explanation_incorrect.D: An esophageal web causes partial obstruction, not a gasless abdomen or the classic TEF presentation.
explanation_incorrect.E: A hiatal hernia is a diaphragmatic defect, not a cause of neonatal esophageal atresia.

educationalObjective: Pure esophageal atresia yields a gasless abdomen, whereas adding a distal TEF yields a prominent gastric bubble.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: An infant has recurrent episodes of cyanosis and coughing during feeding but no esophageal atresia. A contrast study demonstrates a side-to-side connection between the trachea and esophagus resembling the letter H, with contrast passing into the trachea.
question: Which tracheoesophageal anomaly is characterized by an H-shaped fistula without esophageal atresia?
explanation_correct: In the H-type tracheoesophageal fistula, the connection between the trachea and esophagus resembles the letter H and there is no esophageal atresia. Infants can present later with coughing, choking, and cyanotic episodes during feeding and are at risk for recurrent aspiration. Because the esophagus is continuous, a nasogastric tube can often be passed, distinguishing it from the atresia variants. The other anomalies either lack a fistula or involve an interrupted esophagus.

explanation_incorrect.A: Esophageal atresia with distal TEF has an interrupted esophagus and a fistula to the distal segment, not an H-shaped side-to-side connection.
explanation_incorrect.B: Pure esophageal atresia has no fistula at all and produces a gasless abdomen.
explanation_incorrect.C: Esophageal stenosis narrows the lumen without creating an abnormal tracheal connection.
explanation_incorrect.E: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is a pleuroperitoneal membrane defect with bowel in the chest, not a tracheoesophageal fistula.

educationalObjective: An H-type fistula is a side-to-side tracheoesophageal connection without atresia, causing aspiration and cyanotic feeding episodes.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A neonate with esophageal atresia and distal TEF is being evaluated for associated anomalies. The clinician notes the VACTERL association and counsels the family about other organ systems that may be involved.
question: Esophageal atresia with distal TEF is associated with which cluster of defects?

options.text: Cleft lip, cataracts, and congenital heart block
Vertebral, anal, cardiac, renal, and limb defects
Seizures, cafe-au-lait spots, and optic glioma
Webbed neck, bicuspid aortic valve, and short stature

explanation_correct: Esophageal atresia with distal TEF is associated with VATER/VACTERL defects: Vertebral anomalies, Anal atresia, Cardiac defects, Tracheoesophageal fistula, Esophageal atresia, Renal anomalies, and Limb defects. Recognizing this association prompts evaluation of other organ systems in the affected neonate. The other option clusters describe different syndromes such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1, and Turner syndrome. This is a classic association tested with EA/TEF.

explanation_incorrect.A: Cleft lip, cataracts, and congenital heart block are not the VACTERL cluster associated with EA/TEF.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hypertelorism, omphalocele, and macroglossia suggest Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, not VACTERL.
explanation_incorrect.D: Seizures, cafe-au-lait spots, and optic glioma suggest neurofibromatosis type 1, not VACTERL.
explanation_incorrect.E: Webbed neck, bicuspid aortic valve, and short stature suggest Turner syndrome, not VACTERL.

educationalObjective: EA with distal TEF is associated with VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, TEF, esophageal atresia, renal, limb) defects.
